newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs play cat and mouse over polls.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs play cat and mouse over polls.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs are once again playing a familiar cat and mouse game with the international community and this time the issue is supervision of Bosnia's local polls next year, Western officials in Sarajevo said.
"First they sound a negative note publicly and then in subsequent contacts they say they are willing to cooperate," an OSCE official told Reuters on Thursday.
"We understand this to be a tactic on their behalf."

U.S. envoy for Balkan affairs John Kornblum failed on Wednesday to win an agreement from Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic to agree to international supervision of municipal elections, now delayed until spring 1997.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has been in charge of organising elections under the terms of the Dayton peace accord which ended the Bosnian war, but it has yet to secure an extension of mandate to conduct and supervise the local polls.

The OSCE's head of mission, Robert Frowick, announced on Tuesday that the local polls had to be postponed because of continuing political problems, but conceded that the Serbs' reluctance to go forward was decisive.

Tuesday's decision was the second postponement of the troublesome municipal elections, originally delayed in the run up to general elections held on September 14 because of voter registration irregularities.
Bosnia's Moslems and Croats have already signed the mandate extension but the Serbs are yet to be convinced, Frowick said.
But another OSCE official said that, in contacts with Plavsic on Wednesday, he had the impression that she would come to terms.
"We do have a long way ahead (with mandate extension) but she has never closed the door to OSCE supervision," he said.
The United States has accused Plavsic of blocking elections and said it will throw its diplomatic weight behind efforts to have internationally supervised polls next year.
"That will be the result here, and the Bosnian Serbs ought to understand that right now," U.S. State Departement spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
The Serbs mastered the art of political brinksmanship over the 43 months of war, usually succumbing to international pressure after ardous negotiations and often after deadlines had expired.

"Now that hardline nationalists won the September elections and have to backpedal on their proclaimed separatist goals, they have to play a double game -- one statement for their public and a different one for us," a western diplomat said.
The Serbs fear that Moslem refugees could vote them out of power in towns where they now have a majority following a campaign of ethnic cleansing of thousands of non-Serbs during the war.

With no end to the standoff in sight, international negotiators will need to make intensive efforts in the coming weeks to work out clear strategy to win Serb agreement on mandate extension, the diplomat said.
But critics say the international community lost some of its leverage over the Serbs when U.N.-imposed economic sanctions were lifted recently.

It still has ther carrot of millions of dollars worth of reconstruction aid to bargain with. "In the long run, the Bosnian Serbs will have to realise they will suffer if they do not accept the economic aid," an OSCE official said.
